cases.title: Nicaragua BANADES closure and farm credit cuts
cases.point: Managua, where the national development bank BANADES was based (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Under the 1998-2002 ESAF loan the IMF required the National Development Bank to be wound down and directed credit to end (Acevedo, Envío 2008). Envío (1998) reports the IMF demanded BANADES be privatized or closed and that Central Bank credit to it be cut off.

cases.conditions: ESAF 1998-2002 (as listed by Envío, 2008): 'Liquidate at least 80% of the National Development Bank's assets' and 'No use of directed credit policies'; also privatize the grain agency ENABAS. The 1998 letter of intent promised to cancel BANADES' banking licence and channel rural credit through private banks, cooperatives and NGOs. Nicaragua's January 1999 letter of intent to the IMF confirms BANADES 'was liquidated' in June 1998.
cases.community: BANADES, the country's oldest bank (85 years), served more than 80,000 producers in 1990 and fewer than 7,000 in 1997. Bank financing of farming fell from $92.4 million (1990) to $64.5 million (1996). State bank credit covered about 30,000 acres of beans and 88,300 acres of corn in 1990; in 1997 the state financed under 800 acres of beans and 5,800 acres of corn. Envío counted about 300,000 producers without financing (Rocha, Envío, March 1998). Acevedo notes more than 75% of farm jobs are in very small units with little land.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: The government set up a Peasant Credit Fund lending through NGOs and cooperatives, paid for by foreign donors. Envío (1998) says President Alemán later announced he would use what was left of BANADES for a state body for peasants, which went back on the IMF commitment. The IMF agreement said farm credit policies 'were eliminated and will not be reintroduced'.

sources.title: New Twist with the IMF: The Winners and the Losers
Sixteen Years Lost in Five Agreements with the IMF
Nicaragua: Letter of Intent and Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies, January 27, 1999

cases.confidence_note: The drop in BANADES clients (1990-1997) came before the formal closure, during earlier adjustment years; the sources tie the closure itself and the end of directed credit to the IMF program.

cases.title: Senegal 2023 fuel and electricity price rise
cases.point: Dakar, capital (approximate); fare rises were also reported in Bignona

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Raising energy prices was a prior action (a step required before the IMF board meeting) in the January 2023 review of Senegal's Stand-By Arrangement, Standby Credit Facility and Policy Coordination Instrument (IMF Country Report 23/30).

cases.conditions: IMF Country Report 23/30 lists as a prior action: 'Raise energy prices to limit electricity and fuel subsidies to 2.7 percent of GDP in 2023'. Publishing a roadmap to phase out energy subsidies by 2025 was also a prior action. Without action, subsidies were about 4.2% of GDP.
cases.community: From January 2023 electricity rose by 18.97 CFA francs per kWh for low-voltage users and 22.79 for medium-voltage users, and diesel and premium fuel by 100 CFA francs per litre (Enerdata). Seneweb reported a shared-taxi ride in Bignona going from 500 to 1,000 CFA francs, and said bakers, carpenters, tailors and hairdressers faced higher power bills. The minibus operators' union Aftu announced fare rises.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: The transport minister denied any agreed fare rise and said support for operators was being studied; a transport strike was called (Seneweb, 16 January 2023). The government expected to save about 258 billion CFA francs and aimed to end energy subsidies by 2025 (Enerdata). The IMF board completed the review in January 2023.

sources.title: Senegal: Sixth Review under the Policy Coordination Instrument and Third Reviews under the Stand-By Arrangement and the Standby Credit Facility (Country Report No. 23/30)
Press Release No. 23/02: IMF Executive Board completes reviews for Senegal
Senegal will remove energy sector subsidies by 2025
Hausse des prix de l'énergie : Les pauvres vont payer la note

cases.confidence_note: The IMF report gives no per-unit amounts; those come from Enerdata. The Bignona fare figure is a single local report.

cases.title: El Salvador 2025 public wage bill cuts and dismissals
cases.point: San Salvador, capital (approximate); dismissals were spread across ministries, hospitals and town halls

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Extended Fund Facility (EFF) loan. Its first review (IMF Country Report 25/190) credits the early 2025 adjustment to 'visible cuts in the wage bill' and sets a civil service reform benchmark.

cases.conditions: Program fiscal adjustment relying on wage bill cuts (IMF Country Report 25/190, June 2025), with a structural benchmark for a civil service reform to avoid 'unnecessary expansions of public employment'. El Mundo reports the government committed to the IMF to cut wage bill spending by 0.8% of GDP in 2025, 1.3% in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027.
cases.community: The Movement of Dismissed Workers (MTD) counted 17,810 public dismissals in 2025 by September, including 11,200 posts removed in the 2025 budget, 4,214 teacher posts at the Education Ministry, 1,100 staff at the health fund Fosalud, 490 at the San Salvador Este town hall (340 in waste collection) and 83 doctors at the social security institute ISSS (El Mundo, September 2025).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: The MTD called the dismissals arbitrary and illegal and expected more as new bodies took over waste collection, markets and hospitals. The IMF completed the first review in June 2025; pension and civil service reforms are due in 2026.

sources.title: El Salvador: 2025 Article IV Consultation and First Review under the Extended Fund Facility (Country Report No. 25/190)
Organización prevé más despidos en el sector público por implementación de ANDRES, Dirección de Mercados y Red de Hospitales

cases.confidence_note: The IMF sets wage bill targets, not job counts; the dismissal count comes from a workers' group and was not independently checked by El Mundo. Some dismissals come from the government's own restructuring of agencies.

cases.title: Brazil 1999 IMF program social spending cuts
cases.point: Brasília, where protesters gathered outside the World Bank office (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year stand-by credit of SDR 13 billion (about US$18.1 billion) approved 2 December 1998, with primary surplus targets and spending cuts (IMF press release 98/59).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Part of the financing package; in 1999 it also suspended loan disbursements to the states of Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul during their debt dispute with the federal government (Bretton Woods Project).

cases.conditions: Primary surpluses of 2.6% of GDP in 1999, 2.8% in 2000 and 3% in 2001, with 'substantial cuts in discretionary current and capital spending', a higher financial transactions tax and higher pension contributions from public employees; budget savings of about 3.4% of GDP in 1999 (IMF press release 98/59).
cases.community: Social Watch Brazil reports the social area lost R$2.04 billion (23.7%) in 1999 and 25 of 31 worker-funded programs for low-income people were ended. The Bretton Woods Project reports the 1999 land reform budget was cut 42.6% and sanitation 73%, and a rural settlements program was scrapped. Unemployment in Greater São Paulo reached 19.3% in 1999 (DIEESE/SEADE, cited by Social Watch).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: NGOs, unions, students and opposition parties protested outside the World Bank office in Brasília in early 1999. Brazil beat the IMF surplus target; Social Watch notes a R$30 billion primary surplus was absorbed by R$85 billion of federal debt interest (to September 1999).

sources.title: IMF Approves SDR 13 Billion Stand-By Credit for Brazil; Activates NAB (Press Release 98/59)

cases.confidence_note: The IMF set overall surplus and cut targets; the choice of which programs to cut was the government's. Unemployment also reflects the January 1999 currency crisis.

cases.title: Lebanon 2022 electricity tariff rise
cases.point: Beirut, seat of the state utility Électricité du Liban (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Executive Magazine reports World Bank financing for Egyptian gas and Jordanian power imports (about $200 million for the Jordan deal) depended on conditions, one of which required EDL to raise electricity bills. The financing was not delivered.

cases.conditions: Raise EDL electricity tariffs as a condition of proposed World Bank financing for gas and power imports (Executive Magazine, 2024). The IMF's April 2022 staff-level agreement also called for cost-recovery plans in the energy sector, without naming a tariff level.
cases.community: On 1 November 2022 EDL raised tariffs from about 1 US cent per kWh to 10 cents for the first 100 kWh and 27 cents above that (The New Arab). Supply averaged three to six hours a day afterward (Executive Magazine). In a 1,200-household survey, Human Rights Watch found nearly nine in ten households said power costs hurt their ability to pay for other essentials; the poorest fifth went without power 11 hours a day on average.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Executive Magazine reports EDL did raise bills but failed the World Bank's bill-collection requirement, and the import deals did not go ahead. Human Rights Watch urged the IMF to press Lebanon not to raise tariffs until it could guarantee reliable supply.

sources.title: Lebanon raises electricity prices for first time since 1990s
Cut Off From Life Itself: Lebanon's Failure on the Right to Electricity
Press Release No. 22/108: IMF reaches staff-level agreement with Lebanon

cases.confidence_note: Only one source (Executive Magazine) states the World Bank required the tariff rise; The New Arab cites only unnamed donors, and officials said the rise would pay for more fuel and longer supply. The World Bank loan was never made. HRW's household figures cover all power costs, including private generators, not the tariff alone.
